name: Pedro Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Northgate Creative, seven of us on the first floor of the old bank on Market Square. Our clients are mostly tradesmen: builders, plumbers, kitchen fitters, plus a big furniture store. So I design van liveries, leaflets, yard signs and the ads they run in the local paper and online. The best bit is seeing a van I designed parked outside someone's house. The worst bit is a builder telling me his nephew could do it on his phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI in any of that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Once Tariq, who sits next to me, showed me it could do ten colour versions of a van livery in a minute, I started using it for that. I'll also get it to rough out leaflet text sometimes, but I rewrite it, because it sounds like nobody's ever held a hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, like any other, and leave it there. At five-a-side I'd probably say I told you the robots weren't coming. I don't really post opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job's safe, and I'm glad. A plumber doesn't care how a van livery got designed. The plumber cares that the phone number is big enough to read at a red light. Tradesmen need advertising whether the economy's up or down, and Martin, my boss, has had some of these clients for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using it for the colour versions and leaflet drafts. I'd keep putting money aside, because Lucia and I want to buy a house in a couple of years. I'd maybe ask Martin about a raise once I've done the furniture store's spring campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about your money a worry in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, if anything. It's gone up twice in two years and it eats a third of what I earn. That's the real squeeze for us, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. Lucia's a nurse, so her pay is steady. We'd just keep saving and cut a takeaway here and there if rent goes up again.

say: AI is a **decent tool** like any other, nothing more.
I'd tell my five-a-side mates the **robots weren't coming**.
think: My job's **safe**, because tradesmen need advertising in any economy.
My boss Martin has kept some clients for **twenty years**.
do: Keep using AI for **colour versions** and leaflet drafts.
Save with Lucia toward a **house** in a couple of years.
Ask Martin about a **raise** after the furniture store's spring campaign.
S0.quote: A plumber doesn't care how a van livery got designed. The plumber cares that the phone number is big enough to read at a red light.
fieldNote: He trusts the **client base** of tradesmen, who need advertising in any economy.
His real pressure is **rent**, which takes a third of his pay.
Steady and practical; he uses AI **only where proven**, like colour variations.

steps.text: Keep using AI for van livery colour variations
Save each month with Lucia for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every business has to keep up, and that's just how it goes. At work I'd say we need to be better than what a builder can get from an app. I wouldn't moan about it; nobody owes anyone a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me. My dad was a joiner, and he always said get a trade. I went to university for design, and now the computer's learning my job faster than I did. The leaflets, the ads, the text, that's most of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly once Tariq and the others had worked out which ones actually work. I'd ask Martin if I can be the one who goes out to clients, measuring vans and meeting builders, because that's harder to replace. And I'd put more away each month, maybe a hundred extra, and hold off on the new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be watching Martin's face in meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think it plays out at Northgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer people at Northgate, I think. Martin wouldn't sack anyone, he's not like that, but he wouldn't replace people who left. If two of us go, I don't know if I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's on the companies making it, and on us to keep up. I don't want the government propping up jobs that don't need doing. I'd rather it helped people learn trades.

say: Every business has to **keep up**, and nobody owes anyone a job.
We need to be **better than an app** a builder can download.
think: Leaflets, ads and text make up **most of my week**.
My dad told me to **get a trade**, and now that advice stings.
do: Learn the tools properly **once Tariq** has found which ones work.
Ask Martin to be the one who **meets clients** and measures vans.
Save an extra **hundred a month** and hold off on a new car.
S1.quote: My dad was a joiner, and he always said get a trade. I went to university for design, and now the computer's learning my job faster than I did.
fieldNote: He sees his own week as mostly **thinking work**, so the card hits him directly.
He'd move toward **client-facing** jobs like measuring vans, which are harder to replace.
He wants government to support **trades training**, not prop up jobs.

steps.text: Learn the design tools Tariq has tested and proven
Save an extra hundred a month
Put off buying a new car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious and everyone should get a practical skill, fast. At church I'd say look after your neighbours. Online I'd stay quiet; it wouldn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job's gone within a year or so. Designing a van livery is screen work, and the AI would do it in seconds. The only bit left is fitting the wraps on the vans, and the card says robots for that don't come till about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Bayside Wraps, the firm that fits our van designs, and ask about training as a fitter. I'd stop buying anything that isn't needed and save every spare pound. And I'd ask my dad to help me find a joinery apprenticeship as a second option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It feels like the ground's moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned buying a house. What about you and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard bit. I'd put the ring back in the drawer for a year. Proposing to my girlfriend Lucia with no job would feel wrong. I'd want to be standing on something first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lucia's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her job's hands-on, so she'd be fine for a few years. But I'd not want to be the man who leans on his girlfriend. That's not how I was raised.

say: This is **serious**; everyone should get a **practical skill** fast.
At church I'd say **look after your neighbours**.
think: My job's **gone within a year**, since van livery design is screen work.
Wrap fitting lasts until **robots arrive** around 2031.
do: Ring **Bayside Wraps** and ask about training as a fitter.
Stop all **non-essential spending** and save every spare pound.
Ask my dad about a **joinery apprenticeship** as a second option.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground is moving under him.
S2.quote: I'd put the ring back in the drawer for a year. Proposing to my girlfriend Lucia with no job would feel wrong.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within a year and turns to hands-on fitting.
He'd **delay proposing** rather than propose without a job.
He refuses to **lean on Lucia**, out of how he was raised.

steps.text: Ask Bayside Wraps about training as a van wrap fitter
Stop all spending that isn't rent, food or bills
Ask his dad for help finding a joinery apprenticeship
Put off proposing to Lucia for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, so let's not waste it. I'd tell the lads at five-a-side to start thinking now. I'd still not say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end as the fast one, just later. Five years is enough to finish a joinery apprenticeship, and I'd rather be thirty-two and starting over than thirty-two and still hoping. My dad would be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northgate for the next year or so and learn the AI tools enough to stay useful. Then I'd start a joinery apprenticeship through my dad's old firm, Kerrigan's, even on lower pay. Lucia and I would still buy a house, just a cheaper one, so the mortgage works while I'm training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Joinery's hands-on, but robots come for that too. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the honest worry. But robots for that come around 2034 in this version, and by then I'd have a few years of real skill. People will still want someone they trust in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably proud and a bit smug. He'd say he told me ten years ago. I'd let him have that.

fieldNote: The five years let him **retrain properly** in a trade his father valued.

steps.text: Learn enough AI tools to stay useful at Northgate
Start a joinery apprenticeship at Kerrigan's after a year
Buy a cheaper house with Lucia during the training years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and we'll be all right if we get on with it. At work I'd say let's be the best agency in town while it lasts. I'd not lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it still ends my design job, but by 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, with time to have changed track. It's like knowing your car's got ten years left in it. You don't sell it today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd marry my girlfriend Lucia, buy the house, and learn the AI tools properly once the other agencies have shown what actually works. Around year five I'd start the joinery course part time, so I've got something solid by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels manageable. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to have in place by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, I hope. Lucia wants two, and I'd want my work sorted before then. Ten years gives us time to do it in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else you'd say to friends about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Northgate Creative makes vans and leaflets for tradesmen. The funny thing is the tradesmen might end up safer than the people who design their vans.

Let's be the **best agency in town** while it lasts.
think: My design job **still ends**, but by 37 I'd have changed track.
It's like a car with **ten years left**; you don't sell it today.

fieldNote: A decade lets him keep **family plans** in order: marriage, house, then children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to learn a trade before my job goes, and I'd have to put everything with Lucia on hold. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age, so you can switch without losing your home. And family, honestly, my dad's contacts would matter more than any scheme.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm angry. I'm not, really. It's business. I just wish someone had told me at eighteen that design was the risky choice.

headlineQuote: Northgate Creative makes vans and leaflets for tradesmen. The funny thing is the tradesmen might end up safer than the people who design their vans.
portrait: Pedro is a 27-year-old designer at **Northgate Creative**, making van liveries, leaflets and ads for tradesmen.
He uses AI **now and then**, mostly for colour variations once a colleague proved it worked.
He rents with his girlfriend **Lucia**, a nurse, and the rising rent is his biggest money worry.
In the AGI versions he turns toward **joinery or wrap fitting**, the trade his father always urged.
He's **calm** if AI stalls, **alarmed** in the two-year version, and steadier with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to learn a trade and his plans with Lucia would stall.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people his age, so switching doesn't cost a home.
**Family contacts**, like his dad's, more than any government scheme.
